The Long-haired rat (Rattus villosissimus) is an arid-zone murid rodent renowned for its eruptive population dynamics following substantial rainfall events. Respirometry trials conducted under controlled, thermoneutral conditions at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] have yielded a basal metabolic rate of 107 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 107 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns well with predictions for a murid rodent of moderate body size. At this same standard temperature, the gestation period is recorded as 23 days [tg = 23 days], though field observations and captive records indicate a natural range of 22 to 24 days at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively short gestation is typical of small-bodied, rapidly developing murids. The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body mass, with field-captured specimens showing a clear divergence between the sexes.

Adult females of this species attain a maximum recorded body mass of 112 grams [Wwi = 112 grams], while males are considerably heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 156 grams [Wwi = 156 grams]. This degree of dimorphism is consistent with a mating system likely characterized by male-male competition for access to estrous females, a pattern observable in many congeneric rodents. Newborn pups are highly altricial, weighing only 2.3 grams [Wwb = 2.3 grams] at birth, a value that has been extrapolated from data on the closely related Polynesian rat (Rattus exulans) and is consistent with the small neonatal mass expected for rapidly reproducing murid species. This tiny birth mass imposes a significant thermal challenge on the neonates, which are completely dependent on maternal care and huddling for thermoregulation during the initial days postpartum.

During the early postnatal period, the pre-weaning phase is completed relatively quickly. Observations conducted under standard laboratory conditions maintained at a consistent temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] indicate that nutritional independence is achieved at 20 days since birth [tx = 20 days since birth]. This weaning age has been inferred from developmental data for Rattus exulans and fits the typical pattern for altricial murids of a similar metabolic scale, reflecting the comparatively rapid passage through early ontogenetic stages that is characteristic of many opportunistic rodent species adapted to fluctuating environments. The pups transition from a milk-based diet to solid food at this point, although they may continue to occupy the maternal nest for a few additional days to benefit from continued social thermoregulation. The subsequent juvenile growth phase proceeds rapidly. Puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive activation, is reached at 70 days since birth [tp = 70 days since birth] under these same temperature conditions, a developmental schedule that allows young animals to contribute to breeding during favorable periods at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively early sexual maturation is a key life-history adaptation that enables rapid population growth during resource pulses.

Under favorable resource conditions, particularly during the population irruptions known as "plague years," the species exhibits an extraordinary capacity for reproductive output. Data from these boom periods indicate that females produce litters of 5 to 10 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5 to 10 pups per litter], and under these conditions, they can produce a new litter every three weeks, translating to approximately 12 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 12 litters per year]. This maximum reproductive rate is observed when animals are maintained at a consistent body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Combined with the brief gestation of 23 days [tg = 23 days], this fecundity schedule allows a single female to generate dozens of offspring within a single breeding season, fueling the rapid population increases for which this species is well known in its native arid and semi-arid habitats of inland Australia at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C].

Despite the capacity for explosive population growth, the species does not possess an exceptionally long lifespan. Maximum recorded longevity, based on data from related species such as Rattus exulans and observed under controlled captive conditions at a stable core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], is estimated at approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years], or roughly 1825 days. This relatively short life expectancy is consistent with a fast-paced life history strategy, wherein high reproductive output early in life compensates for significant extrinsic mortality pressures in the unpredictable arid environment. The disparity between the small female body mass of 112 grams [Wwi = 112 grams] and the considerably larger male mass of 156 grams [Wwi = 156 grams] further underscores the distinct selective pressures operating on each sex. The overall life history of Rattus villosissimus is thus characterized by rapid development, early reproduction, high fecundity, and a comparatively short lifespan, an adaptive syndrome typical of many opportunistic, colonizing rodent species.
